newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. fails to win probe of alleged Libyan violation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. fails to win probe of alleged Libyan violation.

text.p: The United States displayed film clips, photographs and other items to a U.N. committee on Thursday to show that Libya had tried to import aircraft parts banned under Lockerbie sanctions.
But a U.S. source said opposition by Russia, China, Egypt and France barred any move by the Security Council's Libya sanctions committee to launch an inquiry into the incident.

Libya has been the target of U.N. sanctions since 1992, including an arms embargo and a ban on international flights, for failing to extradite two men wanted by Britain and the United States in the 1988 mid-air bombing of a Pan Am airliner over Lockerbie, Scotland, which killed 270 people.

The United States showed the committee television film clips, photographs and other reports about the August 19, 1996, crash in Belgrade of a Russian commercial IL-76 transport plane soon after it took off with an alleged cargo of 1,000 aircraft tyres, other plane parts and pyrotechnical cartridges, used for ejecting pilots from military aircraft. The cargo was said to have been bound for Malta for onward shipment to Libya.
The U.S. source said the parts were for Yugoslav-made Galeb fighter trainer aircraft, flown only by Yugoslavia and Libya.
Among items displayed was a fuel filter, for use with the Galeb's Rolls-Royce Viper turbojet engines, that was recovered from the wreck of the transport plane.
The source said the United States brought the incident to the attention of the committee only after making several unsuccessful attempts to obtain more information directly from Yugoslavia.

Committee sources said several members of the 15-nation committee spoke in favour of action to probe the matter further. But this was opposed by the four members, who said the evidence relied heavily on media reports and that the incident occurred nearly a year ago.

A Belgrade television report said all 11 people aboard the Russian transport plane perished when it crashed near Belgrade's Surcin airport about three hours after takeoff and after circling the city several times in an attempt to land because of bad weather.

The U.N. sanctions against Libya were toughened in 1993 to include a freeze on some of its assets abroad and a ban on its import of certain types of equipment used at oil terminals and refineries. They do not affect the export of oil from Libya or its purchase of oil-drilling equipment.

A bipartisan group of 53 U.S. senators sent American U.N. envoy Bill Richardson a letter last month urging him to press for an oil embargo. But previous U.S. efforts to get one enacted have failed to win backing in the Security Council. A number of European countries import Libyan oil.

The council issued a mild rebuke last month after a group of Libyans led by their leader, Muammar Gaddafi, flew to Niger and Nigeria aboard four Libyan-registered aircraft, in violation of sanctions. Gaddafi was said to have made the trip to hold prayers marking the Moslem New Year as head of the Islamic Popular Leadership, a group he created in 1989.
